abstract: Snakebites are a public health problem recognized by the World Health Organization as a neglected tropical disease. In Brazil, crotalic venom is considered the most toxic, with a complex composition of bioactive molecules, of which crotoxin (CTX) is the main component. The recommended treatment for snakebite is the use of commercial antivenom produced by hyper-immunizing horses, raising ethical concerns due to repeated venom inoculations that compromise animal welfare and lifespan. This study aimed to design and evaluate a bioinformatically derived peptide (PEP-CTX), corresponding to a putative discontinuous epitope of crotoxin, as an immunogen capable of inducing functional antibodies. Using bioinformatics tools, the peptide PEP-CTX was designed and synthesized by the FMOC Synthesis method. Mice were immunized and at the end of the immunizations, blood was collected, and the immunogenic effect of the peptide was evaluated by ELISA. To evaluate the effects of the serum, produced by PEP-CTX, a venom-induced cytotoxicity assay, and an assessment of phospholipase A2 (PLA2) activity were executed. PEP-CTX induced humoral immune response, generating antibodies that recognized both the PEP-CTX and Crotalus durissus terrificus crude venom. In addition, anti-PEP-CTX serum partially reduced the venom PLA2 activity halo and partially reduced venom-induced cytotoxicity under the experimental conditions evaluated, preserving cell viability, whereas venom incubated with PBS reduced cell viability to approximately 65% of the untreated control. These findings demonstrate that PEP-CTX, designed based on residues from a putative discontinuous epitope of CTX, can induce functionally active antibodies and support the further exploration of epitope-based immunogens as complementary tools for antivenom development.
